673.title: Musa's mother and sister
673.hook: a mother who trusted, a sister who followed along the bank (28:7–13)
673.howItsDone: Muslims retell the story of Musa's mother as a model of trust in Allah's promise, and his sister's quiet watching as a picture of family loyalty; the story is read in surah al-Qasas and surah Ta-Ha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Asiya, and your line: faith in pharaoh's house. Did you protect one small good thing in a hard place? Today, the same baby, from the other end of the river. Day six hundred seventy-three.

Yesterday, Pharaoh's household pulled a chest out of the river, with a baby inside. But someone put that chest in the water. And someone else walked along the bank, watching it float away, keeping far enough back that no one noticed her. Two women at the start of Musa's life, one at each end of the danger. The Qur'an doesn't name either of them. It tells you exactly what each one did.

Surah al-Qasas, verse seven. Pharaoh is killing the boys of the Israelites. Allah inspires Musa's mother: nurse him, and when you fear for him, put him in the river, and don't fear and don't grieve; We'll bring him back to you and make him a messenger. Think about what that asks. The safest place for her son is the very thing a mother would keep him from: moving water. She does it. Verse ten is honest about the cost: her heart became empty, and she nearly gave his secret away, if Allah hadn't steadied her heart. Then the sister. Verse eleven: the mother tells her, follow him. In Arabic, qussihi: track him. She watches from a distance, and, the verse says, they didn't notice her. The chest reaches the palace. The baby refuses every nurse they bring. And the sister steps forward at exactly the right moment: shall I show you a household who'll care for him and wish him well? So Musa goes home, to be nursed by his own mother, now with Pharaoh's protection. Verse thirteen: so that she'd be comforted and not grieve, and know that Allah's promise is true. Here's the detail a scholar enjoys. Qussihi comes from the root q-s-s, to follow tracks. The same root gives qasas, stories, because telling a story is following events step by step. It's the name of this surah. The sister who followed the trail is right inside the word for the whole book of stories. The Hebrew Bible, in later chapters, names the two women Jochebed and Miriam. The Qur'an leaves them unnamed, and remembers every step.
screen: `PUT HIM IN THE RIVER, AND DON'T FEAR.`

segments.voice: The practice: watch over someone quietly. Sit and bring to mind one person who's drifting a little out of reach right now. A teenager, a friend going through something, an elderly parent, a coworker who's gone quiet. You can't carry them. You can walk the bank. Ask: what would quiet watching look like this week? A check-in text with no pressure. Noticing what they need before they ask. Being nearby at the right moment. Choose one. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Qussihi. Follow his tracks: Musa's mother trusted him to the river, and his sister tracked him along the bank, both unnamed, both remembered. Today's word.
Your line: she followed along the bank. Today, do one quiet, unseen thing for the person you thought of, and don't mention it. Day six hundred seventy-three.

674.title: The Queen of Sheba
674.hook: a wise ruler who consulted and chose well (27:23–44)
674.howItsDone: Muslims read the Queen of Sheba's story in surah an-Naml; teachers often point to her as an example of consultation (shura) and wise leadership.

segments.voice: Yesterday, qussihi, and your line: she followed along the bank. Did you do one quiet thing for someone, and keep it quiet? Today, a woman with a whole kingdom watching her. Day six hundred seventy-four.

A letter lands on a queen's desk. Well, the Qur'an says a bird delivered it. It comes from a king, Sulayman, whose army includes people, jinn and birds. It tells her not to be proud, and to come to him in submission. Her chiefs remind her how strong they are, and leave the choice with her. Whatever she does next, a whole kingdom will live with it. Surah an-Naml, the Ant, tells what she did.

First, the hoopoe's report. Verse twenty-three: I found a woman ruling over them, given plenty of everything, and she has a mighty throne. Her people, it adds, worship the sun. The Qur'an never gives her a name; tradition calls her Bilqis. Then the letter arrives, and watch her. She calls it a noble letter. She gathers her chiefs and says: advise me in my affair, I never decide a matter until you're present. They answer: we have strength and great might, but the command is yours. She doesn't take the bait. She says that when kings enter a town, they ruin it and humble its noblest people. So instead of war, she sends a gift, and waits to see how the messengers come back. That's three wise moves in a row: honor the message, consult, test before you strike. Sulayman refuses the gift. She comes to him herself. He's had her throne brought ahead, disguised, and she's asked: is your throne like this? Her answer is careful, almost lawyerly: it is as though it were it. Then a floor of glass she takes for water. And in verse forty-four, her choice: my Lord, I have wronged myself, and I submit, with Sulayman, to Allah, the Lord of the worlds. With Sulayman. Not to him. Commentators notice that word: she stands beside him before Allah. The Qur'an spends more verses on her reasoning than on her wealth. A ruler who listened, refused a needless war, and chose with her eyes open.

The practice: decide something wisely. Bring to mind one decision in front of you, large or small. Then walk it through her steps. First, honor the message: what is actually being asked of me? Second, consult: who should I ask before I decide, and have I asked them? Third, test before you strike: is there a smaller step I could try first, before the big one? Don't decide during the sit. Just see which step you'd been skipping. The bell holds the time.
Bilqis. The name tradition gives the Queen of Sheba, who consulted her council, chose a gift over war, and submitted with Sulayman to Allah. Today's word.
Your line: she chose well. Today, before one decision, ask one person's advice you'd usually skip. Day six hundred seventy-four.

675.title: Hajar, unnamed and remembered
675.hook: unnamed in the Qur'an, remembered by every pilgrim who runs between the hills
675.howItsDone: Pilgrims at the Hajj and 'umrah walk seven times between as-Safa and al-Marwah (the sa'y), with many men jogging between the green markers, and drink Zamzam water, remembering Hajar's search.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bilqis, and your line: she chose well. Whose advice did you ask before deciding? Today, a woman with no kingdom at all, and crowds walking in her footsteps. Day six hundred seventy-five.

Every year at the Hajj, and all year round at the 'umrah, crowds walk back and forth between two low hills in Mecca, as-Safa and al-Marwah. Seven lengths. Along part of the way, green lights mark a stretch where men break into a jog. Grandmothers in wheelchairs are pushed along it. Children ride on shoulders. Every one of them is retracing the steps of a single mother, alone, looking for water. The Qur'an never says her name.

The Qur'an gives the outline. In surah fourteen, Ibrahim prays: our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley with no crops, by Your sacred House. And in al-Baqarah, as-Safa and al-Marwah are named among the signs of Allah. The woman herself is left out. Her name, Hajar, and her story come from a long hadith in al-Bukhari, told by Ibn 'Abbas. Ibrahim brings her and the baby Isma'il to the empty valley with a bag of dates and a skin of water, and turns to go. She follows him. Are you leaving us here, where there's no one and nothing? She asks again and again. He doesn't look back. Then she asks a different question: did Allah command you to do this? He says yes. And she answers: then He will not abandon us. She goes back. The water runs out. The baby cries. She climbs as-Safa to look for anyone, sees no one, hurries down through the valley and up al-Marwah. Seven times. The Prophet ﷺ said, in that same hadith: that is why people go between them. Then she hears a voice, and an angel strikes the ground, and water comes up: Zamzam. She hurries to wall it in with her hands. The Prophet said, may Allah have mercy on the mother of Isma'il; if she'd left it, it would have become a flowing stream. The Bible knows her as Hagar and tells her story in its own way. In Islam, her search became a rite. Unnamed in the book, she sets the pace for every pilgrim.

The practice: think of an unsung person. Sit and let someone come to mind whose effort holds your life up and whose name almost no one knows. The person who cleans your building. A grandparent who crossed a border with nothing. A nurse from years ago. A teacher you never thanked. Picture them doing the work, back and forth, like Hajar between the hills. Say their name if you know it. If you don't, hold their face. If you pray, you can ask for mercy for them. The bell holds the time.
Hajar. Mother of Isma'il, unnamed in the Qur'an, named in hadith: her seven runs between as-Safa and al-Marwah became the sa'y of every pilgrim. Today's word.
Your line: unnamed, never forgotten. Today, learn the name of one person whose work you rely on and haven't noticed, and use it. Day six hundred seventy-five.

676.title: The parables
676.hook: the gnat, the spider, the good tree, the lamp: the book teaches in pictures
676.howItsDone: Muslim teachers and preachers often build lessons around the Qur'an's parables, and the Light Verse (24:35) is among the most recited, discussed and calligraphed passages in Islamic art.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hajar, and your line: unnamed, never forgotten. Whose name did you learn and use? Five days of women in the book are behind us. Today, the way the book teaches. Day six hundred seventy-six.

Some people in early Medina laughed at the Qur'an for mentioning small things. A fly. A spider. Why would the word of God talk about insects? Commentators connect that mockery to a verse in al-Baqarah, which answers without blinking. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! Allah disdaineth not to coin the similitude even of a gnat." Even a gnat. The book isn't embarrassed by small pictures at all. In fact, it's built on them.

The word is mathal: a likeness, a parable, an example. Its plural is amthal. And the Qur'an's usual phrase for making one is daraba mathalan, to strike a parable. Daraba is to strike, and the same verb is used for minting coins, stamping the image into the metal. Pickthall's English happens to keep the picture: Allah coins similitudes. A parable is an idea struck into a picture so it holds its shape. Walk through a few. In surah twenty-nine, people who rely on protectors other than Allah are like a spider that builds itself a house, and the frailest of all houses is the spider's. You've walked through one; you know. In surah fourteen, a good word is like a good tree, roots firm, branches in the sky, fruit in every season, and a bad word like a tree torn up from the ground. And in surah twenty-four, the Light Verse. "Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth." Then the picture: His light is like a niche, and in it a lamp, and the lamp in a glass, and the glass like a shining star, lit from a blessed olive tree, its oil almost glowing on its own. Light upon light. Scholars have filled whole books on that one verse, and still say it isn't exhausted. Several times the Qur'an says why it does this: Allah strikes parables for people so that they might reflect. A rule is forgotten by dinner. A spider's web on the way home reminds you.
screen: `MATHAL: A LIKENESS, STRUCK LIKE A COIN.`

segments.voice: The practice: draw one parable. Find a pen and any scrap of paper. Choose one picture from today: the spider's web, the good tree with its roots and branches, or the lamp in a glass in a niche. Draw it. Badly is fine; nobody will see it. As you draw, go slowly, and let the picture explain itself to you. What makes the web frail? What holds the tree up? Where does the light come from? When you finish, look at it for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Mathal. A likeness, a parable: an idea struck into a picture, like a gnat, a spider's house, a good tree, or a lamp in a niche. Today's word.
Your line: he strikes parables. Today, keep your drawing where you'll see it, and notice one real spider's web, tree or lamp, and let it say what the verse said. Day six hundred seventy-six.

677.title: Justice, again and again
677.hook: justice is commanded again and again, even against yourself (4:135; 5:8)
677.howItsDone: Muslim jurists treat justice ('adl) as a central aim of Islamic law, and 4:135 and 5:8 are often quoted on fairness in testimony, judging and everyday dealing, including with opponents.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mathal, and your line: he strikes parables. Did a web, a tree or a lamp say something to you? Today, a command the book keeps striking, verse after verse. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

Being fair is easy when nothing's at stake. It gets hard in three places. When the truth hurts you. When it hurts someone you love. And when it helps someone you can't stand. It's easy to carve out those three exceptions without ever saying so out loud. Two verses of the Qur'an close them, one by one, and in that order. The second verse even names the third exception directly: the people you hate.

Surah an-Nisa, verse one hundred thirty-five. Believers, be steadfast in justice, witnesses for Allah, even against yourselves, or your parents, or your relatives, whether the person is rich or poor. Look at the order. Yourself first. Then the people closest to you. Then rich and poor, so you can't favor the powerful or pity your way past the truth either. Now al-Ma'idah, verse eight, in Pickthall's translation: "Let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly. Deal justly, that is nearer to your duty." Even the people you hate get a fair hearing. The Qur'an uses two words for this. 'Adl is evenness, setting things level. Qist carries the picture of a fair share, a fair measure, and the book ties it to the balance and the scales. Surah fifty-seven says the messengers were sent with the book and the balance so that people would uphold qist. Commentators tell a story behind a passage in an-Nisa, around verse one hundred five. A man from a Muslim family stole, and his clan tried to pin it on a Jewish man. Verses came down clearing the innocent man and warning against pleading for the guilty. That's the occasion as the commentators report it; the verses themselves speak of not pleading for the treacherous, and of the sin of throwing blame on the innocent. Either way, the pattern holds. In the Qur'an, justice isn't a feeling about who deserves to win. It's a scale you hold level, even when your own hand is on one side of it.

The practice: be fair today. Sit, and think of one disagreement in your life right now, at home, at work, online. Put yourself on the scale first. Where was I wrong, even a little? Then think of the other person. What's the strongest true thing on their side? Don't argue it away. Just set it on the scale beside yours and let it sit there. If you pray, you can ask to be steadfast in justice. The bell holds the time.
Justice. 'Adl and qist: commanded again and again, against yourself and your family, for rich and poor, and even toward people you dislike. Today's word.
Your line: stand for justice. Today, say one true thing in someone's favor that you'd normally leave out, especially someone you don't like. Day six hundred seventy-seven.

678.title: Mercy at every door
678.hook: every surah but one opens with mercy, and mercy is the first name after Allah
678.howItsDone: Muslims recite the bismillah at the start of each surah (except at-Tawbah) and before everyday actions like eating, traveling or starting work, so ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim are names of Allah said many times a day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, justice, and your line: stand for justice. Did you say one true thing in someone's favor? The book holds justice level, and then it does something else at every single door. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

Flip through a printed Qur'an. Every few pages a decorated panel announces a new surah's name, and right under it, one line, the same line, again and again. Bismillahi r-rahmani r-rahim. In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate. One hundred fourteen surahs. Count the doors as you go, and you'll find the line over all of them but one. And you'll find it once more, in a place you wouldn't expect.

The bismillah heads one hundred thirteen surahs. Surah nine, at-Tawbah, has none, and scholars give more than one reason. A report in at-Tirmidhi has the caliph 'Uthman saying it was unclear whether at-Tawbah was its own surah or the continuation of al-Anfal before it, so no line was placed between. Others said a surah opening with a stern declaration doesn't start with that line. Then the unexpected place. In surah twenty-seven, the Queen of Sheba opens a letter from Sulayman, and it begins: in the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate. So the line still appears one hundred fourteen times. Not one is lost. Now look inside the line. After Allah, the first two names are ar-Rahman and ar-Rahim. Both come from the root r-h-m. And rahim, with a slightly different vowel, is the word for a womb. A hadith qudsi in Abu Dawud has Allah saying: I am ar-Rahman; I created the womb and gave it a name from My name. Mercy, in Arabic, sounds like where everyone began. Another hadith, in al-Bukhari and Muslim, says Allah divided mercy into a hundred parts and sent one part to earth. From that one part, creatures are kind to each other, so that a mare lifts her hoof away from her foal. Ninety-nine are kept for the Day. And surah seven: "My mercy embraceth all things." Nearly every door of the book carries the same words over it. Whatever comes after, warnings, laws, stories, the reader walks in under mercy.
screen: `113 DOORS, AND ONE IN A LETTER.`

segments.voice: The practice: count the bismillahs. If there's a Qur'an near you, open it and turn a few pages, just to see the line at the head of each surah. If not, count a different way. Think back over today and count the doors you walked through: waking, eating, leaving the house, starting work, opening a message. How many could have started with that line? Then pick the next door coming up, and if you'd like, say the line quietly now, ahead of it. The bell holds the time.
Bismillah. The line that opens all but one surah, appears inside a letter in surah twenty-seven, and puts the Merciful right after Allah. Today's word.
Your line: mercy first. Today, before one hard conversation, a correction or a complaint, open with something kind, then say the rest. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

679.title: The People of the Book
679.hook: the Qur'an speaks to Jews and Christians as people of scripture, with praise and with argument (2:62; 3:113–114)
679.howItsDone: Muslims use ahl al-kitab for Jews and Christians (and some scholars for others with scripture); classical Islamic law permits eating their food and allows Muslim men to marry Jewish and Christian women, and 29:46 is often quoted on respectful dialogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bismillah, and your line: mercy first. Did one hard conversation open with something kind? Today, how the book speaks to its nearest neighbors. Day six hundred seventy-nine, the end of a week.

Medina, in the time of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, wasn't a town of one faith. There were Jewish tribes with their own neighborhoods, markets and scholars. And Christians came too: once, from Najran, as a delegation that stayed to talk. The Qur'an had a name for all of them, and it wasn't stranger or outsider. It was a name about a book. Ahl al-kitab. The family, or the people, of the scripture.

Ahl means family, household, people. Kitab is book, scripture. The name begins from what they share with Muslims: a revealed book, Torah and Gospel among the scriptures the Qur'an honors. The Qur'an speaks to them in two voices, and it's honest to hear both. Praise, first. Surah three, verses one thirteen and one fourteen: they are not all alike. Among the people of the scripture is an upright community who recite Allah's verses through the night and bow down, who believe and do good and hurry to it. And al-Baqarah, verse sixty-two, names believers, Jews, Christians and Sabaeans, and says whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does right has their reward with their Lord. Muslim scholars read that verse in more than one way, some more narrowly, some more broadly, and the debate is old. Then argument. The Qur'an disputes with Jews and Christians over points of belief, such as who 'Isa was, and it criticizes some of their conduct in its time. It doesn't hide that. But it also sets the manner of the argument. Surah three invites them to a common word: that we worship only Allah. Surah twenty-nine says: don't argue with the people of the scripture except in the best way. And surah five allows Muslims to eat their food, and Muslim men to marry their women. Praise, argument, a shared table. Jews and Christians, of course, describe their own faiths in their own words. This is how the Qur'an speaks to them.

The practice: learn one thing about a neighbor's faith. Sit, and think of a Jewish or Christian person you know, or a congregation you pass, or any faith not your own. What do you actually know about how they pray, or what they read? Notice the gaps without judging them. Pick one question you'd honestly like answered: a holiday, a prayer, a word. Plan to find the answer from them, or from a source of their own, not from someone talking about them. The bell holds the time.
Ahl al-kitab. People of the book, the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians: spoken to with praise, with argument, and in the best way. Today's word.

Your line: people of the book. This week went from she followed along the bank, she chose well, unnamed never forgotten, he strikes parables and stand for justice, to mercy first. Today, ask your one question, kindly. Day six hundred seventy-nine.

it praises an upright community among them who recite through the night (3:113–114).
Muslim scholars read 2:62 in more than one way

fork.setup: a Christian or Jewish neighbor disagrees with you about faith. what manner does surah twenty-nine set?
options: argue only in the best way.
fork.reveal: don't argue with the people of the scripture except in the best way (29:46).

original.note: Arabic: people of the book, people of scripture.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Qur'an treats other faiths as outsiders.
what it means: it names Jews and Christians by their scripture, and speaks to them with praise, argument and courtesy.
what a scholar hears: 2:62 has been read narrowly and broadly since early tafsir; 5:5 grounds the shared table in law.
